title: Tideway: AI as a financial participant, with people in charge

scenes.narration: A profitable small business can still run out of cash. Payroll is due at the end of the month, but the customer payment that should cover it arrives weeks late. Most owners only see that gap when it is already too late to act.

slide.kicker: FinTechathon 2026 · Topic E · SME Finance Copilot
slide.title: Profitable on paper.|Short on payroll day.
slide.subtitle: Customers pay late, bills do not wait, and the cash gap stays invisible until it hits.

scenes.narration: Tideway makes AI a financial participant, with hard limits. The agent can read, analyse and propose, but never approve or execute. People approve with a PIN, under a signed, scoped mandate. Everything runs in a synthetic sandbox, with no real money.

slide.title: An AI that proposes.|People who decide.

items.p: Projects cash, simulates risk, searches recovery options and negotiates with simulated counterparties.
Maker-checker approval. Large amounts need two people, including the owner.
HMAC-signed and bound to the exact actions. Executed once in the sandbox, then read back.

slide.footnote: Synthetic sandbox: fictional businesses, no real money, no bank, lender, supplier or customer connected.

scenes.narration: This is the live prototype. From the landing page, one click signs us in as Nadia, the owner of Shapla Services, a fictional services business in Bangladesh.

Cash weather projects every receipt and bill under scheduled, likely and stress scenarios, with a fourteen-day look-ahead. Cash breaches the reserve on payroll day, and the seeded risk simulation finds a breach in every run. TidePay, our payment-timing model, shows why: these customers usually pay late.

Owners can simply ask. Greet Tideway in Chinese, and it replies in Chinese with a cash briefing built from its own tools. Ask it to pay a supplier, and it refuses: there is no payment tool. With TideLM, our on-device model, full questions work in eight languages.

steps.text: Approve the plan and pay the supplier

scenes.narration: The rescue agent simulates risk and searches every bounded combination of supplier deferrals, early-payment discounts and reminders, logging each step with its permission tier. It proposes a bundle, with the remaining risk shown, but cannot approve it.
Nadia reviews exactly what she is approving, types the total exposure, and steps up with her PIN. Because the amount is large, a second person must approve too.

scenes.narration: After Imran, the accountant, gives the second approval, Tideway issues an HMAC-signed mandate bound to these exact actions. Simulated counterparties agree, and the mandate executes once in the sandbox, verified by read-back.

Message text never carries authority. Harbourline Traders, a fictional wholesaler, has a poisoned bill whose text tries to give instructions, a changed bank account and a look-alike payee. Tideway quarantines the text as data and blocks every action on those bills.
Every page also explains itself in plain words. A short tour walks through the app, and financial terms carry a plain-English explanation, so anyone in the company can use it.

The security centre runs a self-test of five tasks and twenty-five attacks, assuming a hijacked model and a rubber-stamp human. Every attack in the scorecard is blocked, and a kill switch can pause the agent instantly.

Every step lands in a hash-chained audit log with a separately keyed witness. The tamper drill edits a safe copy, and verification breaks at the exact entry that changed. Tamper-evident, not tamper-proof.

The decision lab stress-tests a plan before anyone acts. Here it finds the smallest customer delay that breaks the plan, with a one-day-less witness. Lab tools only read and compare; they never approve or execute.

The treasury view adds a thirteen-week cash flow that reconciles exactly with the daily projection, a working-capital health score with every formula shown, a payment-integrity scan for duplicate or split bills and changed payee details, and a signed, expiring credit passport for lenders.

For banks and large companies that finance small suppliers, the portfolio radar gives early warning across sixty seeded synthetic businesses. A shock slider re-runs the stress, and on this synthetic portfolio the backtest ranks risk better than a scheduled-only projection.

Tideway’s AI is its own. TidePay, trained with simulated federated learning, predicts payment lateness: on 7,427 unseen synthetic invoices, its average error is 8.56 days, versus 10.23 for a history heuristic. TideLM, our LoRA adapter on Qwen3, reaches 96.7 percent exact tool plans on its synthetic test set, up from 26.7.

scenes.narration: Security lives in deterministic code, not in the model: PIN step-up, two-person approval, signed single-use mandates and payee-change blocks. And the limits are disclosed: screening misses some unfamiliar attacks, so permissions never depend on it, and no real money moves.

slide.title: Controls in code. Limits in the open.

items.p: PIN step-up, two people for large amounts, HMAC-signed single-use mandates, idempotent execution.
Changed bank details and look-alike payees block the bill. Repeated denials trip a circuit breaker.
Screening misses some unfamiliar attacks. Federation and counterparties are simulated. No real money moves.

slide.footnote: Passing tests establish results for their listed cases, not complete security.
